title: Large Language Models and User Trust: Consequence of Self-Referential Learning Loop and the Deskilling of Health Care Professionals
pub: Journal of Medical Internet Research, vol. 26, e56764 (2024)
author: Avishek Choudhury · Zaira Chaudhry

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core case for assistive rather than autonomous deployment, with expert verification, oversight and continuing human accountability. It materially extends that position by proposing a prospective feedback loop in which reliance weakens practitioner skill while AI-generated training data reduce model quality, sharpening the cluster’s concerns about verification capacity and professional development. These mechanisms are conceptual predictions, not established effects.
qs: Addressing this requires fostering a symbiotic relationship between human intellect and LLM capabilities, ensuring AI augments rather than replaces human intellect.

Our discussion highlights a potential feedback loop where LLMs, increasingly trained on narrower data sets dominated by their own outputs, may experience a decline in output quality coinciding with a reduction in user skills.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s concern that delegating cognitively demanding work can weaken the expertise needed for later oversight, especially during professional training. It also reinforces the distinction between accountability and effective control: clinicians may remain legally and morally responsible as final decision-makers, but the source does not establish that this status alone gives them effective control over LLM-assisted care. Its deskilling claims are conditional and conceptual rather than empirical.
qs: Instead, the concern is more pronounced for the *next generation* of health care professionals — particularly medical students who might increasingly use AI for educational tasks, where over-delegating could attenuate the development of critical analytical skills and a comprehensive understanding of medical concepts traditionally cultivated through deep engagement.

Clinicians, operating at the interface of LLM recommendations and patient care, are generally seen as the final decision-makers, thus bearing primary moral and legal responsibility, grounded in the principle that clinicians must integrate LLM outputs into a broader clinical judgment context.

kp.k: Conceptual feedback loop links trust, deskilling, and model degradation
kp.d: In this health care viewpoint published 25 April 2024, Choudhury and Chaudhry conceptually propose that growing clinician reliance, declining human skill, and increasing use of AI-generated training content could reinforce one another. The projected trajectories in Figure 1 are anticipated risks, not reported longitudinal findings; the authors explicitly describe the feedback loop as theoretical.
qs: In this paper, we conceptually investigate the dynamics between clinicians' growing trust in LLMs, the evolving sources of training data, and the resultant implications for both clinician competency and LLM performance over time.

While theoretical at this stage, this feedback loop poses a significant challenge as the integration of LLMs in health care deepens, emphasizing the need for proactive dialogue and strategic measures to ensure the safe and effective use of LLM technology.

kp.k: Expertise enables error detection but remains task-specific
kp.d: The authors argue that clinicians can delegate routine tasks while using domain expertise to verify and correct outputs. Users seeking help precisely because they lack knowledge are more vulnerable to persuasive inaccuracies. A general practitioner handling an atypical dermatological case illustrates that professional status alone does not ensure sufficient expertise for verification.
qs: Subject matter experts (doctors) may use LLMs to handle routine, time-consuming tasks, with the advantage of being able to critically evaluate output, verify accuracy against clinical standards, and make corrections.
A general practitioner facing an atypical dermatological case may lack the specialized knowledge to critically evaluate the validity of the LLM's output — an environment where trust becomes critical.

kp.k: Verification costs may offset automation's workload savings
kp.d: The paper identifies a conditional productivity constraint rather than measuring net time savings: checking AI-generated work can consume the time saved by delegation. It frames balancing accuracy and productivity as central to clinical adoption.
qs: A pivotal consideration is whether verification of LLM outcomes by health care staff negates the purported reduction in workload: if professionals must meticulously check each AI-generated output, time saved through automation may be offset by time spent on verification.

kp.k: Trust can undermine verification even among capable clinicians
kp.d: The authors distinguish the ability to verify from willingness to do so. They argue that blind trust can produce automation bias, reinforce confirmation bias when recommendations agree with a diagnosis, and generate what they call precautionary bias when disagreement prompts clinicians to defer to the model over their own judgment.
qs: A user may have the ability and expertise but be unwilling to review LLM output due to prior trust or biases.
When LLM recommendations align with a clinician's initial diagnosis (agreement), confirmation bias can be reinforced, leading to a narrowed diagnostic vision.

Conversely, in cases of disagreement, precautionary bias can occur: the clinician, having developed reliance on the LLM, might doubt their own expertise and perceive the LLM to be the safer alternative.

kp.k: Self-generated training content could entrench bias and homogeneity
kp.d: The authors hypothesize that widespread LLM use for writing, educational materials, summarization, and risk identification could feed model-generated content back into training, diluting original human insights and degrading performance. They argue that stringent quality assurance in health care fine-tuning may mitigate this risk while still reinforcing particular clinical approaches reflected in curated data.
qs: This paradox occurs when AI-generated human-like content becomes so widespread that the AI begins to reference its own generated content, potentially leading to an echo-chamber effect where original, human-generated insights become diluted or harder to distinguish.
Consequences include the propagation of biases, increased homogeneity in generated data, and ultimately hindered performance.

When LLMs are fine-tuned for health care applications (e.g., Med-PaLM), severity can be mitigated through stringent quality assurance, but the risk can shift toward reinforcement and entrenchment of specific clinical approaches and schools of thought, reflecting biases in the curated data.

kp.k: Deskilling concerns particularly involve future professional formation
kp.d: Reduced practice and immediate AI answers could weaken learning, analytical development, and diagnostic competence. The authors explicitly avoid predicting definite deskilling among established practitioners, whose training and experience provide a foundation. Their stronger concern concerns medical students and future clinicians whose foundational skills may never develop fully if educational and diagnostic work is over-delegated.
qs: As individuals come to rely more on LLMs for routine tasks — such as the synthesis of patient information or the interpretation of medical data — there is a possibility that their skills may diminish over time due to reduced practice.

It is crucial to note that the discussion does not assert that LLMs will definitively lead to the deskilling of *current* practitioners: these professionals have developed expertise through extensive experience and rigorous academic training, establishing a solid foundation not readily compromised by AI tools.

Instead, the concern is more pronounced for the *next generation* of health care professionals — particularly medical students who might increasingly use AI for educational tasks, where over-delegating could attenuate the development of critical analytical skills and a comprehensive understanding of medical concepts traditionally cultivated through deep engagement.

kp.k: Skill priorities shift while manual fallback remains important
kp.d: The paper warns that future clinicians accustomed to AI-led diagnostic review could struggle with manual chart review during AI failures. It advocates complementary deployment and describes a shift toward problem-solving, critical thinking, creativity, and patient rapport rather than reliance on memory-based tasks.
qs: If future generations of clinicians grow accustomed to AI doing the bulk of diagnostic review and analysis, their own diagnostic skills might not develop as fully; should they be required to review patient charts manually due to AI failures, they may find the task daunting.
The advent of human-AI collaboration prompts a shift in skill-set emphasis toward problem-solving, critical thinking, creativity, and patient rapport over reliance on memory and knowledge-base tasks.

kp.k: Clinical accountability involves clinicians, providers, and institutions
kp.d: The authors characterize clinicians as generally retaining primary moral and legal responsibility as final decision-makers, while identifying unresolved shared-liability questions where model errors cause harm. They connect provider responsibility to training-data accuracy, disclosure, and user support, and institutional responsibility to safe integration, tool selection, training, and oversight. This is a conceptual medicolegal discussion, not a report of adjudicated liability.
qs: Clinicians, operating at the interface of LLM recommendations and patient care, are generally seen as the final decision-makers, thus bearing primary moral and legal responsibility, grounded in the principle that clinicians must integrate LLM outputs into a broader clinical judgment context.
Determining the extent of provider liability hinges on the accuracy of training data, transparency about capabilities and limitations, and adequacy of user training and support.
Institutional policies — selection of AI tools, clinician training, oversight mechanisms — are pivotal in mitigating risks.

kp.k: Legislative frameworks and transparency should support critical engagement
kp.d: The authors present the Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2023 and the Artificial Intelligence Accountability Act as legislative steps toward standardized procedures and assessment frameworks. They advocate ethical responsiveness and argue that transparency can counter algorithmic deference by supporting comparison of outputs with professional expertise and patient-specific circumstances.
qs: The Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2023 and the Artificial Intelligence Accountability Act represent a critical legislative step toward ensuring responsible use of algorithms, calling for standardized procedures and assessment frameworks.

Ensuring transparency in LLMs can enhance trust by making the AI's reasoning visible, combating algorithmic deference by encouraging professionals to critically assess outputs against their expertise and patient-specific contexts.

kp.k: Changing model performance requires continuing oversight and assistive boundaries
kp.d: The authors caution that current performance cannot guarantee future performance as training data change. Their concluding recommendation is continuing evaluation, robust oversight, and explicit limits that position LLMs as assistance for professionals rather than independent clinical decision-makers.
qs: It is important to acknowledge that the performance of LLMs like ChatGPT today does not guarantee their performance tomorrow; performance is temporal and will change as new data are fed to the algorithm.

This underpins the necessity for robust oversight mechanisms, ongoing evaluation of AI-driven outputs for accuracy and relevance, and clear guidelines on the role of LLMs as assistive tools rather than stand-alone decision-makers.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Choudhury and Chaudhry argue that LLMs can augment clinical work, but predict conditional risks from verification burdens, excessive trust, self-referential training, and the underdevelopment of future clinicians' skills.
pts.d: The source concerns health care, not legal-service delivery. The authors claim that expert clinicians can delegate routine tasks while checking and correcting outputs, although verification may offset automation's workload savings. They argue that blind trust can reinforce confirmation bias when AI agrees with a diagnosis and precautionary bias when it disagrees, potentially causing clinicians to defer to AI over their own judgment. They anticipate a self-referential learning loop in which increasingly prevalent AI-generated training content dilutes original human insights, entrenches biases, increases homogeneity, and degrades model performance. Habitual delegation may reduce practice and motivation for deeper learning, with particular concern for the development of medical students and future clinicians rather than a definitive prediction of deskilling among established practitioners. They also argue that LLM use complicates medical liability: clinicians remain final decision-makers, while providers and institutions face questions about shared responsibility. Their preferred model is augmentation with human oversight, not autonomous clinical decision-making.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims are presented principally as conceptual arguments and anticipated risks in a viewpoint, not as findings from an original empirical study.
pts.d: Choudhury and Chaudhry explicitly describe their investigation as conceptual and the self-referential loop as theoretical. Figure 1 illustrates a projected trajectory linking rising trust, declining skill retention, changing training-data composition, and eventual model-performance decline; it is not reported as a measured longitudinal relationship. The supplied document provides no quantified productivity gains, verification costs, deskilling effects, or model-performance deterioration. A general practitioner handling an atypical dermatological case illustrates limits to domain expertise, rather than documenting an observed clinical incident. Med-PaLM is an example used in discussing fine-tuning and quality assurance, not a benchmark result. The accountability discussion invokes traditional liability principles and named legislative efforts, including the Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2023 and the Artificial Intelligence Accountability Act, rather than presenting adjudicated cases or measured regulatory effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The April 2024 viewpoint distinguishes current deployment from longer-term, conditional risks and gives no calendar date for a tipping point.
pts.d: The authors describe LLM use as already occurring, but anticipate that deeper adoption and growing dependence on AI-generated training data could produce a future self-referential zone and user deskilling zone. These are conceptual stages without a quantified timetable. Productivity benefits depend on relevant expertise and willingness to verify outputs; possessing expertise alone does not ensure review. Deskilling is a possibility associated with reduced practice and over-delegation, not an inevitable consequence for current practitioners, whose established training and experience are acknowledged as protective. Concern is stronger for future clinicians whose analytical skills are still developing. Stringent quality assurance in health-care fine-tuning may mitigate self-referential risks, although curated data may reinforce particular clinical approaches. The authors stress that present model performance does not establish future performance and call for continuing oversight.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include expert and nonexpert users, medical students and future clinicians, patients, health care institutions, and LLM providers.
pts.d: Expert clinicians may gain time by delegating routine tasks but must retain the ability and willingness to verify outputs. Users without relevant expertise, including clinicians working outside a specialty, are more vulnerable to persuasive inaccuracies. Medical students and future practitioners face the predicted risk of weaker analytical and diagnostic skill formation and reduced ability to work manually during AI failures. Patients face downstream consequences for diagnostic accuracy, treatment, safety, and quality of care. Clinicians are described as bearing primary moral and legal responsibility as final decision-makers; provider responsibility depends on such factors as training-data accuracy, transparency, and support, while institutions are responsible for safe integration, tool selection, training, and oversight. The authors also anticipate a shift in clinical skill emphasis toward problem-solving, critical thinking, creativity, and patient rapport.
